The answers to great questions often lead to even greater questions, requiring ever grander answers. The loop continues, which each round getting larger until finally the question sought is either a question of everything, or a question that man is incapable of asking because he cannot even fathom what the question itself ought to ask. In some cases, the sheer scope of circumstances limits the loop to just a single round. That is the case with the question "Are we alone?"

For decades, people had done all sorts of reckoning to try and answer that question. The tools of religion, mathematics, science, and philosophy all tried to grasp at the question. It should have come as no surprise when the answer did come to us when a star freighter landed in a wheat field in western Kentucky. Many of us would have been happy if it had been greys or little green men; something similar to us but not quite us. Others would have hoped for a truly alien appearance to emerge, as would be suggested by statistical change and evolutionary demands of alien worlds. Instead, what came out was a practical carbon copy of man.

What differentiated humans from the Uzid -- as they called themselves -- were only a few physiological things. A modified skeletal structure that enabled them to transition quickly from low gravity transport to the gravity of moons and planets. A more efficient cardiovascular and respiratory system that allowed them to survive in both low and high pressure systems, and even survive (to an improved extent) the vacuums of space or being submerged. At the cellular level it was discovered that they lacked mitochondria, with energy generation being handled purely by enzymatic processes around the organelles, which surprisingly turned out to be more efficient than if they had mitochondria. Beyond those changes and a few small others, they were human. Far more technologically advanced than us, but the genetic testing proved that they were human.

The main divergence was social, not physical. They did not claim any planet, moon, or star as their home. They were the equivalent of nomads, just wandering the cosmos in their giant star freighters that were more akin to giant flying cities. When their cities become crowded, they expanded the star freighters. When the star freighters became too big, they split in half. A few scientists and philosophers noted this and pondered if the star freighters weren't a life form of their own that reproduced via mitosis. Technology had changed the Uzid. They were diverse in appearance, but lacked any distinguishing features of race as racial divisions had largely been bred out over numerous generations. Similarly war was just as far removed for them. They knew how to fight and they could still prove violent if angered, but their behavior was more akin to bees defending a hive rather than a Roman conquest for glory and land.

The Uzids also have the concept of the uyma. To a human, it is an inconceivable concept surrounding the nature of space and the cosmos itself. An absolute enigma. It is the knowledge of the uyma that allows them to travel the cosmos and survive; a social and scientific knowledge that without one just stalls on the cusp of realizing the next level of reality and physics. The humans have a similarly alien concept to the Uzids; an idea that we take for granted.

"I'll be back." An absolutely inconceivable phrase to an Uzid. Socially they cherish every moment with each other, because given the uncertainties of space, there is no promise that they will see each other again after they part ways. They never assume there will be a next time, that they will meet again. They acknowledge that it happens, but there is never a promise or guarantee attached to it. It is a phrase that instills comfort in humans, but perpetuates a most primal of fears in the Uzid because of their understanding of the uncertainty of the world. I once made the mistake of telling my Uzid wife that I would return from work, only to return finding her in the same place as I left her, a look of absolute relief in her face as I walked in through the door to my home. She had waited for me just like a dog might wait for its master -- unable to conceive that separation can just be a temporal blip and not an entire lifetime.

Slowly as the two races continue to co-exist, children will be born between the humans and Uzids. And maybe by being raised by two similar yet different mindsets, the children will be able to fathom both the uyma and the promise of return. Or maybe the two are mutually exclusive, and thus a possible reason that certain questions can't be conceived is because we conceived of a different question that precludes reasoning the other.

Stranded on a planet, you must build a factory to defend yourself and rebuild your ship: Factorio. [Non-traditional RTS, resource/logistics management]

I'm definitely not a marketer, someone could probably come up with a better title so I want to talk a little more about this game.

Factorio is an alpha-stage game that's very playable. The devs are super active, the last update was April 4th. You start off on a planet not much else than a pickaxe and start to mine. This is where the similarities to Minecraft and the like end.

You then build a miner. Then you build another miner to provide fuel for the first miner using conveyer belts and grappling arms. You'll keep doing this until you build a power plant, and then you can power your miners. The more equipment you use, the more pollution you'll create, and thus the more aliens will attack you. You'll need to start up a production chain to make bullets for your turrets. You'll need to start up a train depot and train system to get resources from farther away. Eventually you'll have robots doing your work for you while you hunt down alien nests with a rocket launcher, grenades, and attack robots.

There's technically a way to 'win' this game, but one could easily keep playing and making their system more efficient. If you like Skylines, Tropico, Banished or any resource/logistics management games like I do, Factorio is worth a play.

Note that I don't work for the Factorio devs or get anything out of this other than spreading word of mouth about a game that i love. I have not seen it featured on any site so far and hope that it get some atention here.
